ACTION: ADD
TITLE: One model, one objective: encoder, cross-channel mixing and query decoder trained together
PROPOSAL: We build a forecaster whose three parts are designed for each other. The encoder is a channel-independent patch transformer; after it, a low-rank mixing layer lets each variate attend to a small set of learned channel prototypes rather than to all other variates, which keeps the cross-channel step linear in the number of channels. The decoder is a set of learned horizon queries that cross-attend to the encoded patches and to the prototypes, replacing the flat linear projection. Training is single-stage: in every batch a random subset of input patches is masked and the same decoder must both reconstruct them and predict the horizon, so the auxiliary task uses the decoder that serves at test time. We evaluate on ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Weather, Electricity, Traffic and Solar at horizons 96, 192, 336 and 720 with mean squared and mean absolute error.
CONTROLS: PatchTST, DLinear and TiDE as channel-independent references, iTransformer, Crossformer and TimeMixer as channel-dependent references, the full model with each of the three parts removed in turn, a two-stage counterpart with masked pretraining followed by fine-tuning at equal total epochs, matched parameter counts, three seeds, and measured throughput per epoch.
COST: 48
PREDICTION: The joint model should beat PatchTST on Electricity and Traffic, where cross-channel structure matters, and match it on the ETT sets, with throughput close to PatchTST. The gain could vanish if the prototype mixing collapses onto a single prototype, which the ablation would reveal.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Replacing the linear projection head with an autoregressive patch decoder
PROPOSAL: We keep a channel-independent patch encoder fixed and vary only the decoder. The candidate is a small causal transformer that generates future patches one at a time, conditioned on the encoded past through cross-attention, with teacher forcing during training and scheduled sampling in the last epochs to limit exposure bias. We compare it with the standard linear projection and with a multilayer head of matched parameter count on ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Weather, Electricity and Traffic at horizons 96, 192, 336 and 720, and we report error per horizon step to see whether the decoder helps mostly at long range. We also measure inference latency, since autoregressive decoding adds sequential steps.
CONTROLS: Linear projection on the same encoder, a two-layer feed-forward head with matched parameters, the autoregressive decoder without scheduled sampling, a non-autoregressive query decoder with the same depth, DLinear and PatchTST as external references, three seeds, and bootstrap intervals over test windows.
COST: 36
PREDICTION: The autoregressive decoder should lower error at horizon 720 on Weather and Electricity by a few percent and leave horizon 96 unchanged. It could lose on the ETT sets, where error accumulation over many generated patches outweighs the extra capacity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Masked-future prediction as a single-stage objective aligned with the forecaster
PROPOSAL: Instead of pretraining an encoder by reconstructing masked past segments and then fine-tuning for forecasting, we train the whole forecaster once with an objective whose shape matches inference. Each training window is extended by the horizon, the future part is always masked, and a random fraction of the past is masked as well, so that the model learns to fill temporal gaps and to extrapolate with the same decoder. The loss is the mean squared error on all masked positions, with the future positions weighted up over the course of training. We apply this to a PatchTST encoder with a query decoder on ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Weather, Electricity, Traffic and Solar at horizons 96, 192, 336 and 720.
CONTROLS: Supervised training with the forecasting loss only, two-stage masked pretraining followed by fine-tuning at equal total epochs, the single-stage objective with past masking removed, three past-mask ratios, a placebo auxiliary task that reconstructs shuffled patches, three seeds, and the error curves over epochs for every variant.
COST: 40
PREDICTION: The single-stage objective should match or beat the two-stage pipeline at every horizon with a shorter total schedule, and the past-mask ablation should show that the gap-filling term is what helps. The approach could fail on Traffic, where the strong daily periodicity makes plain supervised training already saturate.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learned sparse channel graphs for cheap cross-variate dependencies
PROPOSAL: We test whether cross-channel information can be exploited at a fraction of the cost of full channel attention. Each variate is encoded independently with a patch transformer, and a sparse channel graph is learned from the training data: every variate keeps edges to its k most correlated variates under a lagged correlation measure, and the encoded representations are mixed along those edges with a single message-passing layer. The graph is fixed before training, so the mixing step scales with k rather than with the square of the channel count. We evaluate on Electricity, Traffic, Solar and Weather, which have many channels, and on the four ETT sets, at horizons 96, 192, 336 and 720, and we report error together with wall-clock throughput and peak memory.
CONTROLS: PatchTST without mixing, iTransformer and Crossformer as full channel attention references, a random graph with the same degree as placebo, a dense graph with all edges, graphs at k of 4, 8 and 16, mixing applied before rather than after the encoder, three seeds, and bootstrap intervals over test windows.
COST: 56
PREDICTION: Sparse mixing should recover most of the gain of full channel attention on Electricity and Traffic at a small fraction of its memory, and leave the ETT sets unchanged. If the random graph does as well as the correlated graph, the gain comes from extra capacity rather than from structure.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cross-channel interaction placed in the decoder instead of the encoder
PROPOSAL: Channel-dependent encoders pay for interaction at every layer. We move the interaction to the decoding stage: a channel-independent encoder produces per-variate representations, and a decoder of learned horizon queries attends first over time within each variate and then, once per query, across variates with a single low-rank attention block. The cross-variate step therefore runs on the compressed query representations rather than on all patches, which bounds its cost by the horizon length times the channel count. The model is trained end to end with a forecasting loss. We evaluate on ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Weather, Electricity, Traffic and Solar at horizons 96, 192, 336 and 720 with mean squared and mean absolute error, and we measure peak memory and throughput against channel-dependent encoders.
CONTROLS: PatchTST and DLinear as channel-independent references, iTransformer and Crossformer as channel-dependent references, the same decoder without the cross-variate block, the cross-variate block moved into the encoder, a placebo block that attends across shuffled variates, matched parameter counts, three seeds, and bootstrap intervals over test windows.
COST: 44
PREDICTION: Decoder-side interaction should match iTransformer on Electricity and Traffic at a fraction of its memory and beat it on the ETT sets, where full channel attention overfits. The placebo would reveal whether the gain is structural or comes from the extra parameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Coarse-to-fine decoding of the forecast horizon
PROPOSAL: We decode the future at several temporal resolutions. The encoder, a channel-independent patch transformer, produces representations of the past. A first decoder head predicts the horizon at a coarse resolution, one value per block of 24 steps, from learned block queries. A second head refines each block into its full-resolution values, conditioning on the coarse prediction and on the encoded past through cross-attention. We train both heads together with a loss on both resolutions, and we let the coarse loss dominate early in training so that the model learns the low-frequency shape first. We run the experiment on ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Weather, Electricity, Traffic and Solar at horizons 96, 192, 336 and 720, and we report mean squared error at both resolutions and per horizon step.
CONTROLS: Linear projection on the same encoder, a single-resolution query decoder of matched parameter count, the coarse head alone with linear upsampling, the two heads trained without the coarse loss, DLinear and PatchTST as external references, three seeds, and bootstrap intervals over test windows.
COST: 32
PREDICTION: Coarse-to-fine decoding should lower error at horizons 336 and 720 on Weather and Electricity, where long-range shape dominates, while matching the linear head at 96. It could fail on ETTm1 and ETTm2, whose high-frequency content a coarse head cannot represent and a refinement head cannot recover.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A temporal masking curriculum for one-stage forecaster training
PROPOSAL: We train a channel-independent patch encoder with a query decoder in one stage under a curriculum over what is masked. Early epochs mask short random spans of the input and ask the decoder to fill them, which teaches local dynamics; later epochs mask progressively longer contiguous spans at the end of the input, which converges on the forecasting task itself. The horizon loss is present throughout and the span-filling loss is faded out at the end, so the final model is trained exactly as it is used. We evaluate on ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Weather, Electricity, Traffic and Solar at horizons 96, 192, 336 and 720, and we track validation error over epochs to see where the curriculum helps.
CONTROLS: Plain supervised training, two-stage masked pretraining followed by fine-tuning at equal total epochs, the curriculum reversed from long to short spans, a fixed mask length throughout, a placebo curriculum that masks random non-contiguous patches, three seeds, and bootstrap intervals over test windows.
COST: 40
PREDICTION: The curriculum should beat plain supervised training by a small but consistent amount across horizons and match the two-stage pipeline with fewer total epochs. It could fail on Traffic, where plain training already fits the periodic structure and the curriculum only slows convergence.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Shared decoder for gap filling and extrapolation in forecasting models
PROPOSAL: Train a single decoder to serve both as the reconstruction head during masked training and as the forecasting head at inference, so that what the auxiliary task teaches is what the forecaster uses. The encoder is a channel-independent patch transformer; the decoder is a set of position-indexed queries that attend to visible patches, with the same weights whether a query targets a masked past position or a future position. Each batch mixes both query types, and the loss is mean squared error over all targets. We compare this against the usual design in which pretraining uses a reconstruction head that is discarded before fine-tuning. Evaluation covers ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Weather, Electricity, Traffic and Solar at horizons 96, 192, 336 and 720, with mean squared and mean absolute error and the number of epochs to reach the best validation error.
CONTROLS: Supervised training only, two-stage pretraining with a separate reconstruction head, the shared decoder trained on future queries only, separate decoders for the two query types with matched parameters, a placebo that trains the past queries on shuffled targets, three seeds, and bootstrap intervals.
COST: 36
PREDICTION: The shared decoder should reach the two-stage pipeline's error in fewer total epochs and beat it at horizon 720 on Electricity and Weather. If separate decoders do as well, sharing is not what helps and the benefit comes from the mixed targets alone.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Frequency-domain query decoding for long-horizon forecasting
PROPOSAL: We replace the linear projection with a decoder that predicts the future in the frequency domain. A channel-independent patch encoder summarizes the past; a set of learned queries, one per retained frequency band, cross-attends to the encoded patches and outputs the amplitude and phase of that band over the horizon; an inverse transform assembles the forecast. The number of bands is chosen from the training data so that the retained bands explain most of the energy of the targets. The model is trained end to end with mean squared error in the time domain plus a small penalty on the band coefficients. We evaluate on ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Weather, Electricity, Traffic and Solar at horizons 96, 192, 336 and 720, and we report error separately on the low-frequency and high-frequency parts of the targets.
CONTROLS: Linear projection on the same encoder, a time-domain query decoder with matched parameters, the frequency decoder with all bands retained, the frequency decoder with randomly chosen bands as placebo, FEDformer and DLinear as external references, three seeds, and bootstrap intervals over test windows.
COST: 40
PREDICTION: Frequency decoding should lower error at horizons 336 and 720 on Electricity and Traffic, whose targets are dominated by a few bands, and leave the ETT sets roughly unchanged. It could fail on Weather, where the energy is spread across many bands and truncation discards useful content.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Correlation-prior channel mixing as a fixed, cheap cross-variate step
PROPOSAL: We ask whether a cross-variate step with no learned parameters can capture most of what channel-dependent encoders capture. Before training we estimate the lagged correlation matrix between variates on the training split, keep its leading components, and use the resulting projection as a fixed mixing operator applied to the encoded representations of a channel-independent patch encoder before the forecasting head. The operator costs one small matrix product per time step and adds no parameters. We evaluate on Electricity, Traffic, Solar and Weather, which have many variates, and on the four ETT sets, at horizons 96, 192, 336 and 720, reporting mean squared and mean absolute error, throughput and peak memory, and we compare the fixed operator with a learned one of the same shape.
CONTROLS: PatchTST without mixing, iTransformer and Crossformer as channel-dependent references, a learned mixing matrix of the same rank, a random fixed matrix as placebo, the operator built from contemporaneous rather than lagged correlation, three ranks, three seeds, and bootstrap intervals over test windows.
COST: 28
PREDICTION: The fixed operator should recover a large share of the channel-dependent gain on Electricity and Traffic at almost no extra cost, and the learned operator should add little beyond it. If the random matrix does as well, the gain is an artifact of extra mixing rather than of correlation structure.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Joint encoder, prototype mixing and query decoder under a single objective
PROPOSAL: We train a forecaster whose parts are designed together: a channel-independent patch encoder, a low-rank mixing layer in which each variate attends to a small set of learned channel prototypes, a decoder of learned horizon queries that cross-attend to encoded patches and prototypes, and a single-stage objective that masks random input patches and has the same decoder reconstruct them while predicting the horizon. We evaluate on ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Weather, Electricity, Traffic and Solar at horizons 96, 192, 336 and 720 with mean squared and mean absolute error, together with throughput and peak memory per epoch.
CONTROLS: PatchTST, DLinear and TiDE as channel-independent references, iTransformer, Crossformer and TimeMixer as channel-dependent references, the full model with the mixing layer, the query decoder and the masking term removed in turn, a two-stage counterpart with masked pretraining then fine-tuning at equal total epochs, all models at matched parameter counts, identical lookback and batch size, three seeds, and bootstrap intervals over test windows.
COST: 48
PREDICTION: The joint model should beat PatchTST on Electricity and Traffic and match it on the ETT sets at throughput close to PatchTST. If removing the mixing layer changes nothing on the many-channel sets, the cross-channel claim fails even if the headline error is lower.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: An integrated forecaster with prototype channel mixing and horizon queries
PROPOSAL: We propose a forecaster in which encoding, decoding and training are chosen as one design. A channel-independent patch encoder feeds a mixing layer where every variate attends to a small set of learned prototypes, the decoder consists of learned horizon queries that cross-attend to the encoded patches, and training proceeds in a single stage whose loss combines the horizon error with reconstruction of randomly masked input patches by the same decoder. We report mean squared and mean absolute error on ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Weather, Electricity, Traffic and Solar at horizons 96, 192, 336 and 720, with the best configuration selected on the validation split of each dataset.
CONTROLS: Learning rates over a grid of five values, batch size at three settings, patch length at three values, dropout at three levels, the number of prototypes at four values, instance normalization on and off, warmup length at two settings, the default configuration as the reference at matched epochs, loss curves on training and validation for every configuration, the best validation configuration as the ceiling for every other setting, peak memory per configuration, three seeds, and bootstrap intervals over test windows.
COST: 48
PREDICTION: The best configuration should fall at the middle patch length and a moderate prototype count on most datasets, with error varying by a few percent across the grid. If the validation and test rankings disagree across the grid, the selection is unstable and the reported error must be read with that caveat.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Sparse learned channel graphs against full channel attention
PROPOSAL: We test whether cross-channel structure can be exploited with a cost linear in the channel count. Each variate is encoded by a shared patch transformer, a sparse graph connects every variate to its most correlated peers under a lagged correlation measure fixed before training, and one message-passing layer mixes the encoded representations along the edges. We evaluate on Electricity, Traffic, Solar and Weather, which carry many channels, and on ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1 and ETTm2 at horizons 96, 192, 336 and 720, reporting error, throughput and peak memory, and we ask whether the sparse graph recovers the gain of full attention where that gain exists.
CONTROLS: PatchTST with no mixing as the floor, iTransformer and Crossformer as full channel attention references at measured memory, a dense graph with all edges, a random graph of equal degree as placebo, a graph built from shuffled channels, mixing placed before rather than after the encoder, matched parameter counts, three seeds, and bootstrap intervals over test windows.
COST: 56
PREDICTION: Sparse mixing should recover most of the full-attention gain on Electricity and Traffic at a fraction of its memory and change nothing on the ETT sets. If the random graph matches the correlated graph, the gain comes from capacity rather than from channel structure and the claim fails.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Message passing over a correlation graph for multivariate forecasting
PROPOSAL: We add a single graph layer to a channel-independent forecaster. Variates are encoded separately by a shared patch transformer, a graph is built once from lagged correlations on the training split by keeping each variate's strongest neighbors, and a message-passing layer mixes the per-variate representations along the retained edges before the forecasting head. The design keeps the cross-channel step proportional to the number of edges rather than to the square of the channel count. We evaluate on Electricity, Traffic, Solar and Weather, which have many channels, and on ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1 and ETTm2 at horizons 96, 192, 336 and 720, and we report error, throughput and peak memory for each dataset.
CONTROLS: Neighbor counts at four values, the correlation lag window at three lengths, message aggregation by sum, mean and attention, the graph layer at one, two and three hops, edge weights fixed against learned at matched epochs, dropout on edges at two rates, batch size and memory at each setting, loss curves per configuration, three seeds, and bootstrap intervals over test windows.
COST: 56
PREDICTION: Error should be lowest at a moderate neighbor count and a single hop, with attention aggregation slightly ahead on Traffic. If the choice of lag window changes the ranking of datasets, the graph is sensitive to construction and must be tuned per dataset.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Horizon-query decoding against the linear projection head
PROPOSAL: We hold a channel-independent patch encoder fixed and test whether a decoder of learned horizon queries, one per output patch, cross-attending to the encoded past, predicts better than the flat linear projection. The decoder is non-autoregressive, so inference stays parallel. We evaluate on ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Weather, Electricity, Traffic and Solar at horizons 96, 192, 336 and 720, report mean squared error per horizon step to locate where any gain appears, and measure latency and memory so that the decoder is compared with the linear head at equal inference time.
CONTROLS: Linear projection on the same encoder as the reference, a two-layer feed-forward head with the decoder's parameter count, an autoregressive patch decoder, the query decoder with cross-attention replaced by mean pooling as placebo, PatchTST and DLinear as external references, three seeds, and bootstrap intervals over test windows.
COST: 36
PREDICTION: The query decoder should lower error at horizons 336 and 720 on Weather and Electricity and match the linear head at 96. If the matched feed-forward head gains as much, the benefit is capacity rather than decoding structure and the decoding claim fails.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learned query decoders for multivariate time-series forecasting
PROPOSAL: We study a decoder of learned queries placed on top of a channel-independent patch encoder. Each query stands for one future patch, attends to the encoded past through cross-attention, and is projected to the patch values, with all queries decoded in parallel. We train end to end with mean squared error on ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Weather, Electricity, Traffic and Solar at horizons 96, 192, 336 and 720, and we report mean squared and mean absolute error per dataset and horizon together with inference latency, so that the decoder's accuracy can be read next to its run time on the same hardware.
CONTROLS: Decoder depth at one, two and four layers, query initialization from zeros, random values and sinusoidal positions, two positional encodings for the queries, attention heads at two counts, depth two as the reference at matched parameter counts, dropout at three rates, batch size and peak memory per setting, loss curves per configuration, three seeds, and bootstrap intervals over test windows.
COST: 36
PREDICTION: Two decoder layers with sinusoidal initialization should give the lowest error on most datasets, with depth four overfitting on the ETT sets. If query initialization alone moves error by more than the gap between depths, training is poorly conditioned and warmup must be revisited before any comparison is drawn.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: One-stage masked-future training against the pretrain-then-finetune pipeline
PROPOSAL: We train the full forecaster once with an objective shaped like inference: every window is extended by the horizon, the future part is always masked, a random fraction of the past is masked too, and the same decoder fills both. Future positions are weighted up over training. The model is a PatchTST encoder with a query decoder, evaluated on ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Weather, Electricity, Traffic and Solar at horizons 96, 192, 336 and 720, and we ask whether this single stage matches or beats the two-stage pipeline and whether the gap-filling term is what helps.
CONTROLS: Supervised training with the forecasting loss only as the floor, two-stage masked pretraining followed by fine-tuning at equal total epochs as the reference, the objective with past masking removed, a placebo auxiliary task that reconstructs shuffled patches, three past-mask ratios, the objective applied to an iTransformer encoder to check that the result is not specific to one encoder, loss curves over epochs for every variant, three seeds, and bootstrap intervals over test windows.
COST: 40
PREDICTION: The single-stage objective should match the two-stage pipeline at every horizon in fewer total epochs and beat plain supervised training by a small consistent amount. If the shuffled-patch placebo helps as much, the gain is regularization rather than alignment and the claim fails.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Single-stage training with joint past and future masking for forecasters
PROPOSAL: We replace the pretrain-then-finetune recipe with a single training stage. Each window is extended by the horizon, the future is masked, a random fraction of the past is masked, and a shared query decoder predicts every masked position from the visible past, with future positions weighted up as training proceeds. We use a PatchTST encoder with a query decoder on ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Weather, Electricity, Traffic and Solar at horizons 96, 192, 336 and 720, and we report mean squared and mean absolute error, the number of epochs to the best validation error, and training throughput, so that accuracy and training time are read together.
CONTROLS: Optimizers at two choices, learning rate schedules of cosine and step shape, gradient clipping at two thresholds, total epochs at three lengths, the future weighting ramp at three speeds, mixed precision on and off, batch size at three settings with memory per setting, loss curves on training and validation, three seeds, and bootstrap intervals over test windows.
COST: 40
PREDICTION: The cosine schedule with a slow ramp should reach the best validation error earliest, with mixed precision changing error by less than noise. If results differ across optimizers by more than across seeds, the objective is sensitive to optimization and that sensitivity must be reported with every number.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Full-system evaluation under a fixed, shared protocol
PROPOSAL: We evaluate the integrated forecaster, with prototype mixing, query decoder and single-stage masked objective, under one protocol applied identically to every method: lookback 96, horizons 96, 192, 336 and 720, no dropping of the last incomplete test batch, instance normalization for all, and hyperparameters selected on the validation split with the same grid size for every model. Datasets are ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Weather, Electricity, Traffic and Solar. We report mean squared and mean absolute error, throughput and peak memory, so that accuracy and resource use are read together, and we test whether the gains survive the protocol.
CONTROLS: PatchTST, DLinear, TiDE, iTransformer, Crossformer, TimeMixer and TimesNet rerun under the same protocol rather than copied from papers, each component of our model removed in turn, a two-stage counterpart at equal total epochs, all methods at matched parameter counts and at their published sizes, identical batch size throughout, three seeds, and bootstrap intervals over test windows.
COST: 60
PREDICTION: The integrated model should beat every rerun reference on Electricity and Traffic and tie on the ETT sets. If the rerun references close the gap that published numbers showed, part of the claimed progress in the field is protocol, and we report that as a finding in itself.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Benchmarking the integrated forecaster on eight standard datasets
PROPOSAL: We benchmark the integrated forecaster, which combines prototype channel mixing, a query decoder and single-stage masked training, on ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Weather, Electricity, Traffic and Solar at horizons 96, 192, 336 and 720. We tune on the validation split of each dataset, report mean squared and mean absolute error with throughput and peak memory, and we examine how the error moves with the lookback window, the patch length and the normalization scheme so that practitioners can set the model up on a new dataset with a few runs.
CONTROLS: Lookback windows at four lengths with the shortest as the reference, patch lengths at three values at matched epochs, instance normalization against standard scaling against none, early stopping patience at three settings, the test split evaluated with and without the last incomplete batch, loss curves for every lookback, memory and throughput per setting, three seeds, and bootstrap intervals over test windows.
COST: 60
PREDICTION: Error should fall with longer lookback up to the third length and flatten after, with instance normalization ahead on the ETT sets. If early stopping patience changes the ranking of lookbacks, the validation split is too small and the tuning must move to rolling validation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cross-variate attention moved from the encoder to the decoder
PROPOSAL: We ask whether cross-channel dependencies can be captured once, at decoding time, rather than at every encoder layer. A channel-independent patch encoder produces per-variate representations, and a decoder of learned horizon queries attends over time within each variate and then, once per query, across variates through a single low-rank attention block, so the cross-variate step runs on compressed queries and scales with horizon length times channel count. We train end to end with mean squared error and evaluate on ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Weather, Electricity, Traffic and Solar at horizons 96, 192, 336 and 720, reporting error, throughput and peak memory.
CONTROLS: PatchTST and DLinear as channel-independent references, iTransformer and Crossformer as channel-dependent references at measured memory, the decoder without the cross-variate block, the block moved into the encoder, a placebo block attending over shuffled variates, matched parameter counts, three seeds, and bootstrap intervals.
COST: 44
PREDICTION: Decoder-side attention should match iTransformer on Electricity and Traffic at a fraction of its memory and beat it on the ETT sets. If the placebo gains as much, the block adds capacity rather than structure and the claim fails.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A deeper channel-dependent encoder with full variate and temporal attention
PROPOSAL: We build a channel-dependent encoder that attends jointly over variates and time in every layer, with alternating temporal and variate attention blocks, twelve layers, and a wider model dimension than iTransformer, on the hypothesis that previous channel-dependent encoders lacked depth rather than design. The head is the standard linear projection and training is supervised with mean squared error. We evaluate on ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Weather, Electricity, Traffic and Solar at horizons 96, 192, 336 and 720, reporting error, throughput and peak memory, and we examine whether the extra depth pays off on the sets with many channels.
CONTROLS: iTransformer and Crossformer as shallower channel-dependent references, PatchTST and DLinear as channel-independent references, the encoder at six and twelve layers, variate attention removed as ablation, a placebo with shuffled variates in the variate attention, matched training epochs, three seeds, and bootstrap intervals over test windows.
COST: 44
PREDICTION: The deep encoder should lower error on Electricity and Traffic by a few percent over iTransformer and overfit on the ETT sets. If memory grows faster than accuracy, the design confirms that depth is not the missing ingredient, which is a result in itself.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Decoding the horizon coarse to fine from learned block queries
PROPOSAL: We replace the linear projection with two heads that decode at two resolutions. From a channel-independent patch encoder, learned block queries predict one value per block of 24 future steps; a refinement head then expands each block to full resolution, conditioned on the coarse prediction and on the encoded past through cross-attention. Both heads train together, with the coarse loss weighted up early so the model learns the low-frequency shape first. We evaluate on ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Weather, Electricity, Traffic and Solar at horizons 96, 192, 336 and 720, reporting mean squared error at both resolutions and per horizon step.
CONTROLS: Linear projection on the same encoder, a single-resolution query decoder of matched parameter count, the coarse head alone with linear upsampling, both heads without the coarse loss, DLinear and PatchTST as external references, three seeds, and bootstrap intervals over test windows.
COST: 32
PREDICTION: Coarse-to-fine decoding should lower error at horizons 336 and 720 on Weather and Electricity and match the linear head at 96. It fails on ETTm1 and ETTm2 if the refinement head cannot recover the high-frequency content that the coarse head discards.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: How far the linear projection head goes with a longer lookback
PROPOSAL: We keep the linear projection head and ask how much of the long-horizon error is a matter of context length rather than of decoding. With a channel-independent patch encoder fixed, we vary the lookback from 96 to 1440 steps and measure how error at each horizon falls as context grows, on ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Weather, Electricity, Traffic and Solar at horizons 96, 192, 336 and 720. We fit a saturation curve per dataset and horizon, report the lookback beyond which error stops improving, and compare the memory and throughput price of the longer context with the error reduction, so that practitioners know when more context is worth it.
CONTROLS: DLinear at the same lookbacks, PatchTST at its published lookback, the encoder with and without instance normalization, a placebo that extends the lookback with shuffled older windows, lookbacks at six lengths, three seeds, and bootstrap intervals over test windows.
COST: 32
PREDICTION: Error should fall until a lookback near 720 on the ETT sets and keep falling on Traffic, with memory growing linearly. If the shuffled placebo gains as much as the true lookback, the gain is a normalization effect rather than information from the past.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: One decoder for masked reconstruction and for forecasting
PROPOSAL: We test whether the auxiliary masked task helps more when it trains the very decoder that forecasts. A channel-independent patch encoder feeds a decoder of position-indexed queries that attend to visible patches, with identical weights whether a query targets a masked past position or a future position; each batch mixes both query types and the loss is mean squared error over all targets, in one stage. We evaluate on ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Weather, Electricity, Traffic and Solar at horizons 96, 192, 336 and 720, reporting mean squared and mean absolute error and epochs to the best validation error.
CONTROLS: Supervised training only as the floor, two-stage pretraining with a separate reconstruction head discarded before fine-tuning as the reference, the shared decoder trained on future queries only, separate decoders for the two query types at matched parameters, a placebo that trains past queries on shuffled targets, three seeds, and bootstrap intervals over test windows.
COST: 40
PREDICTION: The shared decoder should reach the two-stage error in fewer total epochs and beat it at horizon 720 on Electricity and Weather. If separate decoders do as well, sharing is not what helps and the benefit comes from mixed targets alone.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scaling masked pretraining of forecasting encoders with a pooled corpus
PROPOSAL: We ask whether the pretrain-then-finetune recipe needs more data than it has had. We pool the training splits of ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Weather, Electricity, Traffic and Solar with public energy and climate series into one corpus, pretrain a channel-independent patch encoder by masked reconstruction on the pooled corpus at three model sizes, then fine-tune on each target dataset with a linear projection head. We evaluate at horizons 96, 192, 336 and 720, reporting mean squared and mean absolute error and the fine-tuning epochs needed, and we fit scaling curves of downstream error against corpus size and model size to see whether pretraining keeps paying off.
CONTROLS: Supervised training from scratch as the floor, pretraining on the target dataset alone as the reference, corpus subsets at three sizes, a placebo pretraining on shuffled series, linear probing against full fine-tuning, three seeds, and bootstrap intervals over test windows.
COST: 40
PREDICTION: Pooled pretraining should lower error on the small ETT sets and change little on Traffic, with the curve flattening at the middle model size. If the shuffled placebo matches real pretraining, reconstruction teaches scale statistics rather than dynamics.

TITLE: A parameter-free cross-variate operator from lagged correlations
PROPOSAL: We ask whether a cross-variate step with no learned parameters recovers most of what channel-dependent encoders gain. Before training we estimate the lagged correlation matrix between variates on the training split, keep its leading components, and apply the resulting projection as a fixed mixing operator to the outputs of a channel-independent patch encoder before the forecasting head. We evaluate on Electricity, Traffic, Solar and Weather, which have many variates, and on ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1 and ETTm2 at horizons 96, 192, 336 and 720, reporting error, throughput and peak memory, and we compare the fixed operator with a learned one of the same shape.
CONTROLS: PatchTST without mixing as the floor, iTransformer and Crossformer as channel-dependent references, a learned mixing matrix of the same rank, a random fixed matrix as placebo, the operator from contemporaneous rather than lagged correlation, three ranks, three seeds, and bootstrap intervals over test windows.
COST: 28
PREDICTION: The fixed operator should recover a large share of the channel-dependent gain on Electricity and Traffic with no extra parameters, and the learned operator should add little. If the random matrix does as well, the gain is extra mixing rather than correlation structure.

TITLE: Zero-shot and few-shot forecasting with a pretrained time-series foundation model
PROPOSAL: We ask how much of the multivariate benchmark a general pretrained forecaster already solves without any architectural work. We run Chronos and TimesFM in zero-shot mode, channel by channel, on Electricity, Traffic, Solar, Weather, ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1 and ETTm2 at horizons 96, 192, 336 and 720, then fine-tune each on a small fraction of every training split with a linear head, and we compare error, throughput and peak memory with trained-from-scratch references. We report where the pretrained models win, by dataset and horizon, so that the value of task-specific design can be read against the value of scale.
CONTROLS: PatchTST, DLinear and iTransformer trained from scratch as references, a seasonal naive forecast as the floor, the pretrained models fine-tuned on the full training split, three fractions of training data for few-shot, a placebo that fine-tunes on shuffled series, three seeds, and bootstrap intervals over test windows.
COST: 28
PREDICTION: Zero-shot models should trail trained references on Traffic and Electricity and come close on the ETT sets, with few-shot closing most of the gap. If fine-tuning on shuffled series helps as much as real data, the gain is calibration of scale rather than learned dynamics.

TITLE: An autoregressive patch decoder against the flat linear head
PROPOSAL: We keep a channel-independent patch encoder fixed and vary the decoder alone. The candidate is a small causal transformer that emits future patches one at a time, conditioned on the encoded past through cross-attention, trained with teacher forcing and with scheduled sampling in the final epochs against exposure bias. We compare it with the linear projection and with a multilayer head of matched parameter count on ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Weather, Electricity and Traffic at horizons 96, 192, 336 and 720, report error per horizon step to see whether gains sit at long range, and measure inference latency, since sequential decoding adds steps.
CONTROLS: Linear projection on the same encoder, a two-layer feed-forward head with matched parameters, the autoregressive decoder without scheduled sampling, a non-autoregressive query decoder of the same depth, a placebo decoder fed shuffled encoded patches, DLinear and PatchTST as external references, three seeds, and bootstrap intervals over test windows.
COST: 36
PREDICTION: The autoregressive decoder should lower error at horizon 720 on Weather and Electricity by a few percent and leave horizon 96 unchanged. It could lose on the ETT sets, where error accumulation over many generated patches outweighs the added capacity.

TITLE: Ensembles and augmentation for channel-independent forecasters
PROPOSAL: We ask how much error a channel-independent forecaster with a linear head can shed through training-time variation alone. We train PatchTST with the standard linear projection under four augmentations, namely jitter, scaling, window warping and frequency masking, and we build ensembles of five members that differ in seed, patch length and augmentation, averaging their forecasts. We evaluate on ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Weather, Electricity and Traffic at horizons 96, 192, 336 and 720, reporting mean squared and mean absolute error per member and per ensemble, the spread across members as an uncertainty estimate, and inference latency, since an ensemble multiplies the forward passes.
CONTROLS: A single PatchTST without augmentation as the floor, each augmentation alone, ensembles of two and five members, an ensemble of identical members with different seeds only, a placebo augmentation that permutes time steps, DLinear and iTransformer as external references, three seeds, and bootstrap intervals over test windows.
COST: 36
PREDICTION: Augmentation should cut error by a few percent on the ETT sets and the ensemble by a few more, with the seed-only ensemble capturing most of it. If the permuting placebo helps as much, the gain is regularization of scale rather than better temporal modeling.
